flashcards.q: What is the one rule that generates the entire iterative linked-list-reversal algorithm?
flashcards.a: Save next_temp = curr.next BEFORE executing curr.next = prev. The overwrite is the only step that destroys your path to the rest of the original list, so it must never happen before the save.

flashcards.q: Why does recursive linked-list reversal cost O(n) space even though iterative reversal is O(1)?
flashcards.a: Recursive reversal performs the same O(n) pointer rewrites, but each recursive call adds one stack frame that isn't released until the full unwind completes -- one frame per node, so O(n) stack space versus O(1) for three scalar pointer variables iteratively.

flashcards.q: Why do range-reversal (LC92) and k-group reversal (LC25) implementations almost always use a dummy/sentinel node before the head?
flashcards.a: You need a pointer to the node immediately BEFORE the segment being reversed so the reversed segment can be spliced back in. A dummy node guarantees this predecessor always exists, avoiding a special case when the range or first group starts at the very head.

flashcards.q: In Reverse Nodes in k-Group (LC25), what must you check BEFORE reversing a group, and what happens if the check fails?
flashcards.a: Confirm at least k nodes remain in the list before starting to reverse that group. Per LC25's spec, if fewer than k nodes remain, that final partial group must be left unreversed in its original order.

flashcards.q: Why is Rotate List (LC61) NOT solved with the reversal pattern despite sounding related?
flashcards.a: Rotation is solved by computing k mod length, finding the new tail/head positions, and relinking three pointers directly (old tail to old head forming a temporary cycle, then breaking it at the new boundary) -- no next-pointer reversal is involved anywhere in the solution.

flashcards.q: Why does reversing a doubly linked list NOT need the three-pointer (prev/curr/next_temp) technique that singly linked reversal requires?
flashcards.a: A doubly linked node never loses its way back after its next pointer is rewritten, because it still holds its prev pointer. You just swap next and prev on every node, then swap the list's head and tail pointers at the end -- a single pass with no temp-save needed.

flashcards.q: In Reorder List (LC143), why must you sever the first half's tail before reversing the second half?
flashcards.a: If the first half's original tail still points into what's about to become the reversed second half, the reversal either creates an unintended cycle or corrupts the reversal's boundary. The split must happen strictly before the reversal step.

flashcards.q: In Reverse Nodes in Even Length Groups (LC2074), what determines whether the final (possibly short) group gets reversed: its originally intended size or its actual remaining size?
flashcards.a: The actual (possibly capped) remaining size. A group intended to be size 4 that only has 3 nodes left is evaluated as size 3 (odd) and left unreversed -- candidates who hardcode the intended size sequence get this wrong.

flashcards.q: What symptom does a buggy reversal implementation show if it overwrites curr.next before saving it to next_temp?
flashcards.a: The result contains only the original head node or a very short prefix -- curr becomes null/None (or gets corrupted into prev's old value) almost immediately because the path forward was destroyed before being captured, so the loop can't advance through the rest of the list.

flashcards.q: In Add Two Numbers II (LC445, digits stored most-significant-first), why might reversing the input lists not be an option, and what's the alternative?
flashcards.a: If the problem disallows modifying the input lists, reversal-in-place isn't available. The alternative is two stacks holding each list's digits, allowing digit-by-digit addition from the least-significant end without touching the original lists' pointers -- trading the O(1)-space property for O(n) space.
